passages.text: Comprehensive Genomic Profiling Reveals the Mutational Spectrum and Clinical Significance of BRCA1/2 and Other Cancer-Susceptibility Genes in Breast Cancer Patients from Southern Tunisia
Simple Summary

Breast cancer is one of the most common cancers among women, but its genetic causes remain poorly characterized in North African populations. <sentence_start/>In this study, we investigated germline genetic variants in 165 Tunisian breast cancer patients using targeted next-generation sequencing of a multigene cancer panel. <sentence_start/>We identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (P/LPVs) in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> genes in 19 patients (11.5%), with several recurrent variants and additional variants not previously reported in our Tunisian cohort. <sentence_start/>P/LPV carriers were more frequently younger at diagnosis and showed significant associations with family history and several clinical features. <sentence_start/>We also identified P/LPVs in other genes. <sentence_start/>In addition, 56 variants of uncertain significance (VUS) were detected, of which 7 were prioritized through computational analyses. <sentence_start/>Additional functional or segregation evidence should be collected to establish pathogenicity. <sentence_start/>Our findings expand the available genetic data on breast cancer in Tunisia and highlight the importance of population-specific genomic studies for improving variant interpretation and genetic counseling.
Abstract

Background/Objectives: This study aims to investigate the mutational spectrum of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> genes in a cohort of breast cancer (BC) patients from southern Tunisia, and to evaluate their clinical and prognostic significance. <sentence_start/>Additionally, this study explores the contribution of other cancer predisposition genes and the prevalence of variants of uncertain significance (VUS). <sentence_start/>Results: Among the 165 patients included, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (P/LPVs) in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1/BRCA2</italic> were identified in 19 cases (11.51%), including 8 in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and 11 in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic>. <sentence_start/>The presence of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> P/LPVs associated with young patients (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.006) and those with TNBC (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.036). <sentence_start/>Beyond <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1/2</italic>, PV/LPVs were detected in other cancer-related genes, including <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3), <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2 cases each), and <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BARD1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">BRIP1</italic> (one case each). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, 56 VUS were identified; among them, 7 were prioritized based on in silico predictive analyses, suggesting a potential deleterious effect. <sentence_start/>However, these VUS should not be used for clinical decision-making without additional evidence from functional and familial segregation studies. <sentence_start/>Conclusions: Our findings provide novel insights into the genetic landscape of breast cancer in southern Tunisia, highlighting the clinical relevance of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1/2</italic> mutations and the contribution of other susceptibility genes. <sentence_start/>These results support the personalized management of breast cancer patients and the implementation of expanded multigene panel testing in routine clinical practice to improve genetic counseling.
1. Introduction

Breast cancer (BC) is one of the leading causes of death worldwide in the female population, with an estimated 2,600,000 cases and 685,000 deaths in 2022 [<citation rid="B1-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers13174287" pmid="34503097" pmcid="PMC8428369" count="1">1</citation>,<citation rid="B2-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jncc.2025.02.002" pmid="40693239" pmcid="PMC12276554" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In Tunisia, the incidence of BC is approximately 30/100,000 per year [<citation rid="B3-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20063673" count="1">3</citation>,<citation rid="B4-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12967-021-02772-y" pmid="33726785" pmcid="PMC7962399" count="1">4</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Several risk factors, such as hormonal regulation and lifestyle, have been associated with BC development [<citation rid="B5-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/tacg.s13139" pmid="23776363" pmcid="PMC3681174" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="B6-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000369571" pmid="25759623" pmcid="PMC4317679" count="1">6</citation>]; however, heredity remains one of the most significant risk factors [<citation rid="B7-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcp.27464" pmid="30552672" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In fact, 5 to 10% of BCs are attributable to hereditary syndromes with autosomal dominant transmission, such as hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC). <sentence_start/>Two major predisposition genes (<italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic>) are responsible for 30-50% of HBOC cases [<citation rid="B8-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7150/jca.30410" pmid="31205572" pmcid="PMC6548160" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> (MIM#113705) and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> (MIM# 600185) are tumor suppressor genes that play a crucial role in DNA repair through the homologous recombination pathway [<citation rid="B8-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7150/jca.30410" pmid="31205572" pmcid="PMC6548160" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Loss of the BRCA function impairs DNA repair, resulting in high mutation rates and thus contributing to tumor development [<citation rid="B9-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/onc.2016.243" pmid="27452521" pmcid="PMC5096687" count="1">9</citation>,<citation rid="B10-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2020.00361" pmid="32269964" pmcid="PMC7109296" count="1">10</citation>].

Indeed, women carrying pathogenic germline mutations in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1/BRCA2</italic> genes have an increased risk of developing HBOC compared to those with wild-type <italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> genes [<citation rid="B8-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7150/jca.30410" pmid="31205572" pmcid="PMC6548160" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="B11-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.6004/jnccn.2021.0001" pmid="33406487" count="1">11</citation>,<citation rid="B12-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers15072132" pmid="37046793" pmcid="PMC10093547" count="1">12</citation>].

Advances in genomics through next-generation sequencing (NGS) have revolutionized cancer diagnosis and management, stratifying risk, guiding surveillance, and informing therapeutic decisions. <sentence_start/>In BC, sequencing is essential for genetic counseling of at-risk relatives, tailored medical follow-up, and eligibility for PARP inhibitor therapies [<citation rid="B3-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20063673" count="1">3</citation>,<citation rid="B4-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12967-021-02772-y" pmid="33726785" pmcid="PMC7962399" count="1">4</citation>].

Thousands of pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants (PV/LPVs) have been identified in the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> genes since they were first studied [<citation rid="B12-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers15072132" pmid="37046793" pmcid="PMC10093547" count="1">12</citation>].

Importantly, the prevalence and spectrum of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1/2</italic> PVs/LPVs vary considerably between different ethnic groups and geographic regions. <sentence_start/>Because of this variability, many population-based studies have been conducted to map the mutational profiles of these genes in various countries [<citation rid="B13-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/gco.0b013e328332dca3" pmid="19841585" count="1">13</citation>,<citation rid="B14-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jncc.2022.12.001" pmid="39036311" pmcid="PMC11256725" count="1">14</citation>].

In the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, where BC incidence, age at onset, and clinical presentation often differ from those of Western populations, characterizing the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1/2</italic> mutational profile is particularly important. <sentence_start/>Studies conducted in several MENA countries have reported the prevalence of germline <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1/2</italic> PVs/LPVs among BC patients, emphasizing both shared and unique variant patterns compared to other populations [<citation rid="B15-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10549-022-06622-3" pmid="35578052" count="1">15</citation>,<citation rid="B16-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.36922/ejmo.5800" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="B17-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-025-09810-5" pmid="40681599" pmcid="PMC12274497" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="B18-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11033-011-0829-8" pmid="21603858" pmcid="PMC3249560" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings bring attention to the need for region-specific genetic testing panels and personalized clinical management approaches.

Tunisia has a complex population history due to its geographical position at the crossroads of North Africa and the Mediterranean. <sentence_start/>Its genetic diversity reflects contributions from North African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and sub-Saharan populations. <sentence_start/>The population also shows varying degrees of endogamy and consanguinity, which may contribute to the persistence of recurrent genetic variants in some communities.

Previous genetic studies have identified both Tunisian-specific and variants shared with other North African and Middle Eastern populations, highlighting the genetic diversity of the region. <sentence_start/>Therefore, characterizing <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 variation specifically in Tunisian patients may help identify recurrent or population-associated variants that could be relevant to genetic testing and clinical management in Tunisia [<citation rid="B19-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1750-1172-7-52" pmid="22908982" pmcid="PMC3495028" count="1">19</citation>].

In Tunisia, previous studies have reported that between 14.1% and 37% of BC patients carry pathogenic <italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> variants [<citation rid="B18-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11033-011-0829-8" pmid="21603858" pmcid="PMC3249560" count="1">18</citation>,<citation rid="B19-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1750-1172-7-52" pmid="22908982" pmcid="PMC3495028" count="1">19</citation>,<citation rid="B20-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.23842" pmid="31209999" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="B21-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12282-016-0693-4" pmid="27025497" count="1">21</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Several recurrent mutations have been identified within this population, suggesting the existence of population-specific mutational patterns [<citation rid="B22-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1684/bdc.2014.2049" pmid="25418591" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Identifying these recurrent variants is crucial for the development of targeted genetic screening strategies and for improving clinical management tailored to the Tunisian context.

The primary objective of this study is to expand the mutational spectrum of the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> genes by identifying germline pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants with or without family history of cancer in patients selected from the south Tunisian region. <sentence_start/>This effort aims to support therapeutic decision-making and provide more effective genetic counseling for Tunisian BC patients and their families.
2. <sentence_start/>Materials and Methods
2.1. Study Population

A cohort of 165 unrelated Tunisian breast cancer patients (162 females and 3 males), enrolled from the Habib Bourguiba Hospital of Sfax-Tunisia’s Medical Oncology Department between 2020 and 2024, was included in this study. <sentence_start/>All patients underwent germline genetic testing based on clinical features, including early onset of breast cancer (<35 years), bilateral disease, triple-negative phenotype, or family history of breast and/or ovarian cancer. <sentence_start/>Among these patients, 116 (70.3%) have a familial history of cancer according to the NCCN guidelines [<citation rid="B11-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.6004/jnccn.2021.0001" pmid="33406487" count="1">11</citation>] and 37/165 (22.4%) were diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).

Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the ethics committee of the Faculty of Medicine of Sfax, Tunisia.
2.2. <sentence_start/>DNA Extraction and Targeted Next-Generation Sequencing

Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood using QIAamp Blood DNA (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. <sentence_start/>Concentration and purity of the DNA were measured using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer and Qubit fluorometer (dsDNA HS kit, Thermo Fisher Waltham, Masachussetts, MA, USA).

DNA libraries were generated using the OncoRisk Cancer Panel (Celemics, Seoul, Republic of Korea) according to the manufacturers’ protocols. <sentence_start/>This panel includes 31 genes: <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BARD1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BLM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BMPR1A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BRIP1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CDH1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CDK4</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">EPCAM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MRE11A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">NBN</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PALB2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PMS2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PRSS1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PTEN</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD51C</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD51D</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SLX4</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SMAD4</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">STK11</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">VHL</italic>.

Sequencing was performed on an Illumina MiSeq Instrument (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) with read lengths of 2 × 151 bp using V3 flow cell (Illumina). <sentence_start/>The average sequencing depth was 1405.85, with a minimum of 100× for variant calling. <sentence_start/>Raw reads were analyzed using the basespace cloud-based tool by Illumina.
2.3. <sentence_start/>Variant Classification

Variants were classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines into five categories: pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variant of uncertain significance (VUS), likely benign, and benign. <sentence_start/>Pathogenicity was assessed after comparing the data with sequence databases: ClinVar (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/), accessed on 1 April 2026, Varsome (https://varsome.com) and Franklin (Qiagen). <sentence_start/>Only pathogenic variants, likely pathogenic variants, and VUS are discussed in this study.
2.4. <sentence_start/>In Silico Pathogenicity Prediction

All VUS identified in this study underwent extended bioinformatic characterization to assess their potential clinical relevance. <sentence_start/>Each VUS was investigated using a panel of computational tools covering different mechanisms: Protein function impact: PolyPhen-2 (probably damaging/benign), SIFT (deleterious/tolerated), Mutation Taster (disease-causing to most sensitive), REVEL, Alpha missense, FATHM, and CADD (Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion); Threshold used: CADD ≥ 20 means potentially pathogenic, in addition to Regulome, SpliceAI, and SPIP, for intronic variants. <sentence_start/>Variants appearing in two or more unrelated patients were flagged as recurrent VUS, potentially indicating founder effects or population enrichment.
2.5. <sentence_start/>Statistical Analysis
Descriptive statistics were generated using SPSS V.30.0.

The following analyses were performed: frequency of PV/LPV and VUS per gene, distribution by age and clinical parameters, comparison of recurrent vs. non-recurrent VUS. <sentence_start/>A <italic toggle="yes">p</italic>-value < 0.05 was considered significant. <sentence_start/>Kaplan-Meier was used to correlate the overall survival in patients carrying or not germline P/LPVs in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1/2</italic> genes.
3. Results
3.1. <sentence_start/>Patient Cohort and Clinical Features

A total of 165 BC patients were enrolled in our study. <sentence_start/>The median age at diagnosis was 43.9 (range, 24-75 years); most were female (98.1%) and all were from the south region of Tunisia. <sentence_start/>A family history of breast and/or ovarian cancer was reported in 70.31% of patients. <sentence_start/>Overall, 92 patients (55.8%) had SBR II invasive ductal carcinoma, 21 patients (12.72%) had bilateral BC and 37 (22.4%) had triple-negative BC. <sentence_start/>Twenty-five patients (15.15%) died of the disease (Table 1).
3.2. <sentence_start/>Pathogenic/Likely Pathogenic Variants

Among 165 BC patients, 19 (11.51%) carried germline <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> (n = 8) and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> (n = 11) P/LPVs, while 10 patients (6.06%) had P/LPVs in other cancer-related genes such as <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, etc. <sentence_start/>(Figure 1). <sentence_start/>Most of these variants had been previously reported in the ClinVar and dbSNP databases, whereas three were novel (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Recurrent PVs in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> (c.8486A>G and c.3248delA) and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> (c.1129del) were each identified in two unrelated patients (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Most P/LPVs were frameshift variants (six in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and five in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic>), while four were missense, two of which were not previously reported in the ClinVar database (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, one patient carried both a frameshift and splice P/LPV in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> (c.1310_1313del./c.632-1G>A). <sentence_start/>Besides <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1/2</italic>, we identified P/LPVs in <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">Chek2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">BRIP1</italic> genes in 10 patients (Table 3). <sentence_start/>It is important to mention that <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic> were considered in the context of breast cancer susceptibility, whereas variants identified in <italic toggle="yes">BRIP1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic> were interpreted according to their established or uncertain gene-disease associations and were not considered evidence of breast cancer predisposition in this cohort.

Interestingly, five patients carried concomitant pathogenic variants, including a pathogenic <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> variant together with an additional pathogenic variant in another cancer-susceptibility gene. <sentence_start/>Notably, all five patients had a strong family history of breast and/or ovarian cancer and were diagnosed at a relatively young age (35-51 years) (Table 2 and Table 3).

Furthermore, we reviewed previously published Tunisian studies, which revealed a heterogeneous <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 mutational spectrum, with several recurrent P/LPVs reported across different cohorts. <sentence_start/>Notably, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> c.211dupA and c.5266dupC, BRCA1 c.5030_5033delCTAA, and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> c.1310_1313delAAGA have been repeatedly identified in Tunisian families or patients (Table 4).
3.3. <sentence_start/>Association of BRCA P/LPV and Clinico-Pathological Features

<italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> status was significantly associated with age at diagnosis, with a higher prevalence of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> mutations among younger patients (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.006, Table 5). <sentence_start/>In addition, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> P/LPVs were significantly associated with a positive family history (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.042), hormonal status (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.036), and presence of metastasis (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.048) (Table 5). <sentence_start/>Survival analysis revealed that carriers of BRCA1/2 pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (P/LPVs) had significantly shorter overall survival than non-carriers (log-rank <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.002; Figure 2A). <sentence_start/>In addition, Cox proportional hazards regression analysis demonstrated that BRCA1/2 mutation status was significantly associated with overall survival (HR = 6.336, 95% CI: 1.745-23.007; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.005; Figure 2B).
3.4. <sentence_start/>Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS)

Several variants of uncertain significance (VUS) were identified across the following genes: <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> (n = 11), <italic toggle="yes">SLX4</italic> (n = 7), <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> (n = 6 each), <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BARD1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic> (n = 3 each), <italic toggle="yes">CDH1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MRE11</italic> (n = 2 each), <italic toggle="yes">BLM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BRIP1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CDNK2A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ERCC1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FANCM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSH3</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PMS2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">NBN</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD51D</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">NSD1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">WT1</italic> (n = 1 each) (Supplementary Table S1). <sentence_start/>Overall, 64 patients (38.7%) harbored VUS distributed across 25 genes. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">SLX4</italic> accounted for the largest number of VUS, with 11 and 7 variants, respectively (Figure 3).

Three recurrent VUS in <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> (p.Phe1463Cys, p.Leu1498Ile, and p.Arg2105Gly) were each identified in two unrelated patients. <sentence_start/>In addition, other recurrent VUS in <italic toggle="yes">BLM</italic> (c.-78del), <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic> (c.583A>G), and <italic toggle="yes">SLX4</italic> (c.-416G>A) were identified in two and four unrelated patients, respectively (Supplementary Table S1).

Co-occurrence of a VUS with a P/LPV in another gene was documented in nine patients. <sentence_start/>Notably, one patient (334) harbored two PVs in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic>, in addition to a VUS in <italic toggle="yes">BLM</italic> (Table 2 and Table 3). <sentence_start/>This patient has a strong family history of BC and is aged 45 years old.

Among the identified VUS, seven variants were considered of particular interest, being predicted as deleterious by in silico prediction tools and/or expected to affect protein function (Table 6). <sentence_start/>They include five missense variants localized in <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic> genes, one novel splicing variant in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic>, and one in-frame delins variant in the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> gene (Table 6).

Two <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> variants (c.4388T>G and c.6313 A>G) were each found in two unrelated patients with a strong family history of BC. <sentence_start/>Both variants sit within the regulatory FAT domain of the ATM protein and are likely to destabilize the protein according to their scores in DynaMutΔΔG of −1.62 and −1.02, respectively. <sentence_start/>Additionally, among the other investigated <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> variants, and based on DynaMut predictions, we found that the Tyr1844Cys may lead to protein destabilization while the Arg2461Cys may have a stabilizing effect (Figure 4).

Furthermore, a novel <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> VUS was identified in a young patient diagnosed at 28 years with a triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). <sentence_start/>Splice-site prediction analysis suggested that this variant may substantially impair the donor splice site (reference score: 82.26; mutated score: 71.06; Δ = −13.62%), indicating a potential disruption of the normal mRNA processing and thus the BRCA2 protein function.

Another novel in-frame deletion-insertion (c.2077_2082delGACAGCinsAACAGT) in exon 10 of the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> gene was detected in one patient diagnosed with breast and ovarian cancer at the age of 40. <sentence_start/>This alteration is predicted to remove two amino acids (Ser694 and Asp695) within the DNA-binding domain of BRCA1 protein, which may have strong implications for the structural stability and the function of the protein.

Importantly, these in silico predictions were used solely to prioritize VUS for further investigation and do not establish their pathogenicity or clinical significance. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, the identified VUS should not be used for clinical decision-making in the absence of additional evidence from functional and familial segregation studies.
4. Discussion

In this study, we report the molecular profiling results of 165 Tunisian BC patients using targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS). <sentence_start/>In total, we identified 29 pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (P/LPVs) distributed across eight cancer-predisposition genes. <sentence_start/>As expected, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> constituted the major altered genes, accounting for 19 out of 29 (65.51%) P/LPVs. <sentence_start/>The remaining variants were distributed amongst <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BARD1,</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRIP1</italic> genes, reflecting the genetic heterogeneity of BC susceptibility in Tunisia.

It is well documented that the prevalence of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> P/LPVs in BC varies considerably among populations due to differences in ethnic background, founder effects, selection criteria, and testing strategies [<citation rid="B13-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/gco.0b013e328332dca3" pmid="19841585" count="1">13</citation>,<citation rid="B14-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jncc.2022.12.001" pmid="39036311" pmcid="PMC11256725" count="1">14</citation>,<citation rid="B18-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11033-011-0829-8" pmid="21603858" pmcid="PMC3249560" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In North African countries, reported frequencies range between 11% to 37%, highlighting both regional heterogeneity and the under-representation of this population in global genetic studies [<citation rid="B15-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10549-022-06622-3" pmid="35578052" count="1">15</citation>,<citation rid="B16-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.36922/ejmo.5800" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="B17-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-025-09810-5" pmid="40681599" pmcid="PMC12274497" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="B18-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11033-011-0829-8" pmid="21603858" pmcid="PMC3249560" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In our cohort, 16 <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PVs were detected in 19 out of 165 patients (11.5%), which aligns with the range of previously reported frequencies for the region [<citation rid="B4-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12967-021-02772-y" pmid="33726785" pmcid="PMC7962399" count="1">4</citation>,<citation rid="B22-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1684/bdc.2014.2049" pmid="25418591" count="1">22</citation>].

Interestingly, three recurrent variants, one in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> (c.1129del) and two in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> (c.8486A>G and c.3248delA), were each found in two unrelated patients. <sentence_start/>Other recurrent <italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> PVs were previously reported in Tunisian BC patients such as c.5030_5033delCTAA in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and c.1310-1313 delAAGA in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> [<citation rid="B4-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12967-021-02772-y" pmid="33726785" pmcid="PMC7962399" count="1">4</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Their recurrence may suggest local founder effects or population-specific mutational hotspots, consistent with prior reports of geographically restricted <italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> variants in North Africa [<citation rid="B18-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11033-011-0829-8" pmid="21603858" pmcid="PMC3249560" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, none of the newly <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 P/LPVs identified in the present cohort overlapped with those reported in this previous cohort. <sentence_start/>This finding indicates that the present study expands, rather than duplicates, the previously reported <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 mutational spectrum in southern Tunisia. <sentence_start/>The identification of additional variants in independent cohorts highlights the genetic heterogeneity of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2-associated BC in the Tunisian population and underscores the value of continued accumulation and harmonization of national genomic data. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, by reviewing the Tunisian literature, we observe a heterogeneous <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 mutational spectrum, with several recurrent variants that may be particularly relevant for developing a national genetic testing strategy. <sentence_start/>Notably, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> c.211dupA and c.5266dupC, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> c.5030_5033delCTAA, and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> c.1310_1313delAAGA have been repeatedly identified in Tunisian families or patients, although their relative frequencies may vary by geographical region and patient-selection criteria.

Moreover, three <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> P/LPVs and two <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> P/LPVs identified in this study have not been previously reported, thereby expanding the mutational landscape of hereditary BC in Tunisian patients and underlining the value of including under-represented populations in global genetic research.

Furthermore, it is important to mention that a comprehensive Tunisian <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 variant resource integrating data from different cohorts and institutions would be particularly valuable for establishing variant frequencies, identifying recurrent or population-enriched variants, and supporting evidence-based genetic counseling and testing strategies.

To further contextualize the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 mutational spectrum observed in our Tunisian cohort, we compared our findings with data reported from neighboring North African populations, particularly Morocco. <sentence_start/>The Moroccan study by Elalaoui et al. [<citation rid="B15-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10549-022-06622-3" pmid="35578052" count="1">15</citation>] analyzed 163 unrelated patients with hereditary breast and/or ovarian cancer and identified a distinct spectrum of recurrent <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 variants, with <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> c.1310_1313delAAGA representing the most frequent variant in their cohort. <sentence_start/>In our cohort, the same <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> c.1310_1313delAAGA variant was identified in one patient, indicating that some PVs are shared across North African populations. <sentence_start/>In addition, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> c.5266dupC, identified in our cohort, has previously been reported among Moroccan patients. <sentence_start/>Conversely, several P/LPVs identified in our cohort were not among the recurrent variants highlighted in the Moroccan cohort, supporting the presence of substantial heterogeneity in the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 mutational spectrum across North African populations.

In our cohort, family history proved to be a strong predictor of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PV status. <sentence_start/>Patients carrying <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2 P/LPVs were significantly more likely to report a family history of breast or ovarian cancer, a finding that is consistent with previously studies [<citation rid="B24-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.6004/jnccn.2022.0030" pmid="35714673" count="1">24</citation>,<citation rid="B25-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1503/cmaj.111670" pmid="22291177" pmcid="PMC3447051" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Moreover, 27% of TNBC patients are <italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> positive, which is in line with reported data [<citation rid="B4-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12967-021-02772-y" pmid="33726785" pmcid="PMC7962399" count="1">4</citation>,<citation rid="B17-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-025-09810-5" pmid="40681599" pmcid="PMC12274497" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="B26-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/(sici)1097-0215(19970807)72:4<599::aid-ijc8>3.0.co;2-l" pmid="9259397" count="1">26</citation>].

Beyond <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>/2, P/LPVs were identified in several additional cancer-related genes, including <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">BRIP1</italic>. <sentence_start/>However, these findings should not be interpreted uniformly as breast cancer-susceptibility variants. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic> have established relevance to hereditary breast cancer risk, whereas the clinical relevance of heterozygous variants in <italic toggle="yes">BRIP1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic> to breast cancer predisposition is not established. <sentence_start/>In particular, <italic toggle="yes">BRIP1</italic> is an established ovarian cancer-susceptibility gene, while heterozygous <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic> variants are primarily associated with carrier status for <italic toggle="yes">MUTYH</italic>-associated polyposis rather than autosomal-dominant hereditary BC. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, these findings were considered as additional germline variants identified through multigene testing rather than as evidence of non-<italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> hereditary BC predisposition [<citation rid="B25-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1503/cmaj.111670" pmid="22291177" pmcid="PMC3447051" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B27-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12672-025-03470-7" pmid="41021100" pmcid="PMC12480218" count="1">27</citation>].

In our cohort, four patients presented the co-occurrence of multiple P/LPVs, and one of them harbored two PVs located in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">RAD50</italic>, together with a VUS located in the <italic toggle="yes">BLM</italic> gene. <sentence_start/>This patient had a strong family history and developed BC at an early age. <sentence_start/>Such findings highlight the complexity of hereditary BC genetics and emphasize the need for careful clinical interpretation when multiple variants are identified.

A substantial number of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) were detected (n = 56), particularly in <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SLX4</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic> genes. <sentence_start/>Based on prediction tools, seven relevant VUS in <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> were retained. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, two <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> VUS were each detected in two unrelated patients. <sentence_start/>These variants are located within the FAT domain and are predicted to affect protein stability and potentially impair ATM protein function. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, additional investigations such as familial segregation studies are required to clarify their pathogenicity and to determine whether they are associated with BC risk. <sentence_start/>We also identified two novel VUS: a frameshift deletion in the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> gene and a splice-site variant in the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> gene, both of which were predicted to affect the function of the corresponding proteins. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> VUS is characterized by the deletion of two amino acids (Ser694 and Asp695) within the DNA-binding domain, potentially altering the structural integrity of the protein. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> variant is predicted to disrupt the donor splice site, and further RNA-based analyses are needed to confirm whether it induces aberrant splicing, including potential exon skipping. <sentence_start/>Numerous studies have concentrated on the reclassification of VUS, especially those occurring in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> genes, which are among the most frequently implicated in hereditary BC [<citation rid="B28-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3892/mco.2021.2385" pmid="34548921" pmcid="PMC8447178" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="B29-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4274/ejbh.galenos.2025.2025-5-2" pmid="40851390" pmcid="PMC12462719" count="1">29</citation>].

Recently, a study of Tunisian BC patients reported the reclassification of two VUS located in <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> (c.6115G>A), and <italic toggle="yes">CHEK2</italic> (c.592+3A>T) genes, into likely pathogenic variants using a combination of familial segregation analysis and comprehensive in silico prediction tools [<citation rid="B30-cancers-18-02810" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fgene.2024.1327894" pmid="38313678" pmcid="PMC10834681" count="1">30</citation>].

While expected in multigene panel studies, the high VUS rate reflects both the genetic heterogeneity of the Tunisian population and the current limitations of international databases, which under-represent North African genomic information, and thus highlights the urgent need for population-specific functional and segregation analyses to clarify its clinical significance, especially in genetically understudied populations such as Tunisia.

This study has some limitations. <sentence_start/>The sample size may not fully represent the genetic diversity of the Tunisian population. <sentence_start/>The gene panel used was limited and might have missed some relevant pathogenic variants. <sentence_start/>Additionally, the identified VUS, and especially the relevant VUS, need further functional validation to clarify their clinical significance. <sentence_start/>Future studies with larger cohorts and expanded panels are needed.
5. <sentence_start/>Conclusions

This study provides a comprehensive molecular characterization of Tunisian BC patients using NGS multigene panel testing. <sentence_start/>By identifying pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants in individuals at high hereditary risk, and by thoroughly annotating and prioritizing variants of uncertain significance (VUS), we reveal both recurrent and novel mutations that point to population-specific genomic patterns. <sentence_start/>The integration of NGS with multiple in silico prediction tools enabled the prioritization of VUS for further investigation; however, these computational predictions do not establish pathogenicity or clinical significance.

Through the generation of such locally relevant genomic data, this work moves Tunisia closer to the implementation of effective precision medicine strategies, where cancer management is adapted to the genetic landscape of the Tunisian population.
